title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
authors: Riccardo Molteni, Minjun Jeon, Paolo Braccia, Abhinav Deshpande, Vedran Dunjko, Liang Jiang
abstract: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Hamiltonian embeddings encode labeled training data into a parameterized Hamiltonian whose approximate ground state defines a classifier.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects quantum training with either classical or quantum inference, offering a route to testing supervised learning on quantum hardware.
method: Encode the classical training dataset into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian.
Optimize Hamiltonian parameters using efficient gradient-estimation methods.
Approximate the ground state with a quantum algorithm and use it for classification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports generalization guarantees, cryptography-based expressivity results, and a demonstration on IBM Heron processors using an unnamed standard benchmark dataset.
infographic.watch_item: Efficient ground-state approximation and practical end-to-end advantage remain implementation concerns; the abstract does not report comparative accuracy or runtime.
infographic.paper_title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings

title: Quantum Broker: QoS-Aware Distribution of Quantum Computations
authors: Giuseppe Bisicchia, Alessandro Bocci, Jose Garcia-Alonso, Juan Manuel Murillo, Antonio Brogi
abstract: Cloud-accessible quantum computing has made heterogeneous Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) available through provider platforms that differ in qubit technology, calibration state, queueing behavior, and pricing model. This heterogeneity makes execution management a quantum-engineering concern: a quantum circuit may be executable on several backends, but the resulting cost, latency, fidelity, and reproducibility depend on backend selection and on how measurement shots are allocated. This paper presents the Quantum Broker, an open-source and provider-agnostic framework for Quality-of-Service-aware quantum execution management. The framework operationalizes shot-wise distribution by exploiting the statistical independence of quantum measurement shots to dispatch a single circuit across multiple heterogeneous QPUs according to user-defined constraints and optimization objectives. It combines a modular execution architecture, interchangeable backend-profiling strategies, and the Quantum QoS Specification Language (QQSpec), a declarative language for expressing QoS requirements. Dispatch planning is supported by two solver backends: a mixed-integer linear-programming (MILP) solver, and a nonlinear dual-annealing solver. Experiments on benchmark quantum circuits and noisy simulator backends show that the Quantum Broker can produce feasible QoS-aware dispatch plans under heterogeneous backend conditions and can improve QoS satisfaction with respect to single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines. The results also expose a practical trade-off between planning time and dispatch quality, with the nonlinear solver producing higher-quality allocations at increased computational cost. Overall, the Quantum Broker provides an extensible execution-management layer for engineering portable, reproducible, and QoS-aware quantum software over fragmented quantum cloud infrastructures.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Broker allocates a circuit’s measurement shots across heterogeneous QPUs to meet user-defined quality-of-service constraints and objectives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its provider-agnostic execution layer helps engineers manage cost, latency, fidelity, and reproducibility across fragmented quantum cloud platforms.
method: Exploit shot independence to distribute one circuit across multiple QPUs.
Express QoS requirements declaratively with QQSpec and profile available backends.
Optimize shot allocations using MILP or nonlinear dual-annealing solvers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmark-circuit experiments on noisy simulator backends produced feasible QoS-aware plans and improved QoS satisfaction over single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The nonlinear solver improves allocation quality at higher planning cost; evaluation on noisy simulators does not establish performance on live QPUs.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Broker: QoS-Aware Distribution of Quantum Computations

title: CO$Φ$ - COmpiling PHotonics into dIgital quantum circuits
authors: Grzegorz Czelusta, Marcin Markiewicz, Jakub Mielczarek, Artur Miroszewski
abstract: Photonic and qubit-based (digital) approaches to quantum computing are largely regarded as separate paradigms. This article aims to bridge these paradigms by developing a method for mapping quantum-optical systems onto qubit-based quantum circuits. The key ingredient enabling this mapping is the introduction of a truncation of the Fock space describing single-mode optical states. Within this framework, representations of basic photonic operations are developed, including the phase-rotation operator, the displacement operator, the squeezing operator, and the beam splitter. Explicit quantum circuit constructions are provided for Fock-space truncations of dimension $N=2$ and $N=4$. We discuss benchmarking of the implemented operations and identify the regime of applicability and the limitations of the proposed method. The presented results can be used to simulate quantum optical circuits on qubit-based quantum computers, with special relevance to Gaussian Boson Sampling in the low-photon-number regime. To demonstrate the practical applicability of this approach, we complement the theoretical framework with a Python-based quantum programming tool CO$Φ$ that compiles Blackbird quantum-optics programs into qubit-based OpenQASM circuits using a truncated Fock-space encoding. The compiler is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Quantum-Cosmos-Lab/cophi.

infographic.key_insight: COΦ maps photonic quantum operations onto qubit-based circuits by encoding optical states in a truncated Fock space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The Python compiler translates Blackbird quantum-optics programs into OpenQASM, enabling photonic-circuit simulation on digital quantum computers.
method: Truncate each optical mode’s Fock space for qubit encoding.
Construct representations of phase rotation, displacement, squeezing, and beam-splitter operations.
Provide explicit circuits for truncation dimensions N=2 and N=4.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports explicit circuit constructions and discusses operation benchmarking, but provides no quantitative accuracy or hardware-performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Finite Fock-space truncation limits fidelity when higher-photon-number states become significant, making the approach most relevant to low-photon-number regimes.
infographic.paper_title: CO$Φ$ - COmpiling PHotonics into dIgital quantum circuits

title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
authors: Andrew J. Ochoa, Martin J. A. Schuetz, Helmut G. Katzgraber
abstract: We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.

infographic.key_insight: Classical Houdayer cluster updates amplify the diversity of quantum-generated maximum independent set solutions by up to 11,923×, with a median gain of 24.3×.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Post-processing can extract more distinct optimal configurations from existing quantum measurements and sometimes improve solution quality.
method: Seed solution sets with measurements from QuEra’s Aquila Rydberg-atom device.
Apply classical Houdayer cluster updates to expand the solution sets.
Use known ground-state degeneracies to measure manifold coverage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 43 problem instances, post-processing recovered a median 21% of the ground-state manifold and provably recovered all of it for six instances.
infographic.watch_item: The method is non-ergodic, so complete ground-state manifold coverage is not guaranteed.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates

title: Ensemble basis-free coherence for quantum communication
authors: Aleksei Kodukhov
abstract: The resource theory of coherence quantifies the quantum properties of states and their role in quantum information processing. Extending coherence theory to ensembles, the natural objects in quantum communication, remains an active research direction, with their operational potential still being explored. In this work, we establish a maximally coherent ensemble in every finite dimension: the continuous ensemble of pure states distributed according to the normalized Haar measure attains the tight upper bound on basis-free relative entropy ensemble coherence. We then prove that ensemble coherence bounds the effective informational advantage of postselective measurements over the Holevo quantity for two equiprobable pure states. Finally, for the qubit B92 QKD protocol, we show that the coherence of Alice's ensemble upper-bounds the secret key rate in the asymptotic regime. These results give ensemble coherence a quantitative operational meaning in quantum communication and cryptography

infographic.key_insight: Haar-distributed pure-state ensembles maximize basis-free relative entropy ensemble coherence in any finite dimension, linking coherence to quantum communication limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ensemble coherence provides theoretical upper bounds on postselection-enabled information gains and the asymptotic secret key rate of qubit B92 QKD.
method: Prove that the normalized Haar ensemble attains a tight coherence upper bound.
Bound the informational advantage of postselective measurements over the Holevo quantity for two equiprobable pure states.
Derive a coherence-based upper bound on the asymptotic B92 secret key rate.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical proofs, with no experimental data or numerical benchmarks described.
infographic.watch_item: The results do not establish achievable rates or practical performance under finite-key and hardware-noise constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Ensemble basis-free coherence for quantum communication

title: Higher-order Parity Constraints for Quantum Approximate Optimization
authors: Anita Weidinger, Glen Bigan Mbeng, Roeland ter Hoeven, Wolfgang Lechner
abstract: The Parity Architecture was originally introduced in the context of quantum optimization algorithms to overcome hardware connectivity constraints. Here, we show that its benefits extend beyond this role by identifying specific parity transformations that enhance the success probability of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for optimization problems defined on hardware-native and sparse graphs. Numerical simulations suggest that this enhancement originates from the higher-order operators introduced by the Parity representation, which accelerate the propagation of correlations across the physical device. We investigate this mechanism for the Signed Max-Cut problem on 3-regular graph instances and demonstrate its practical relevance on IBM Heron quantum processors. QAOA parameters are first classically optimized on small training instances containing up to 14 vertices and subsequently transferred to larger instances executed on quantum hardware. We consider Signed Max-Cut instances of up to 40 vertices and find that, together with an error mitigation technique, the parity-based QAOA identifies the optimal solutions for all the considered 40-vertex instances, whereas the conventional QAOA fails under the same conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Higher-order parity constraints can improve QAOA success probabilities beyond addressing hardware connectivity, apparently by accelerating correlation propagation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Parity-based QAOA offers a promising route to better optimization on quantum hardware using parameters trained on smaller instances.
method: Apply selected parity transformations to Signed Max-Cut on 3-regular graphs.
Classically optimize QAOA parameters on training instances with up to 14 vertices, then transfer them to larger instances.
Evaluate parity-based and conventional QAOA on IBM Heron processors, incorporating error mitigation.
infographic.evidence_signal: With error mitigation, parity-based QAOA found optimal solutions for all tested 40-vertex instances, whereas conventional QAOA failed under the same conditions.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the tested problem family and instances; broader scaling and robustness to hardware noise remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Higher-order Parity Constraints for Quantum Approximate Optimization

title: Shot Allocation Strategies in Debugging Quantum Circuits
authors: Era Thaqi, Coco Gong, Margaret Martonosi
abstract: Debugging quantum programs remains challenging due to the nature of quantum measurement. As quantum algorithms and systems scale, it is increasingly crucial to develop rigorous debugging and verification approaches. Statistical assertion-based debugging validates quantum program behavior through repeated circuit execution and statistical hypothesis testing, but existing frameworks treat shot count as a fixed input parameter, leaving the problem of optimal shot allocation across multiple mid-circuit assertions unexplored. To improve debugging efficiency by making better use of given shot counts, this paper proposes and evaluates four shot allocation strategies within the QDB quantum debugger implemented within the CUDA-Q framework. These allocation approaches: equal split, static weight allocation, adaptive entropy routing, and sequential retirement, use statistical approaches to test whether qubits have expected state characteristics at different points in execution. We evaluate these allocation strategies on different circuits, under both noise-free and depolarizing noise conditions. We show how adaptive strategies use shots efficiently by concentrating them on assertions with high uncertainty. This substantially reduces total shot usage while maintaining comparable debugging confidence.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive shot allocation can reduce quantum debugging executions by focusing measurements on uncertain assertions while maintaining comparable debugging confidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Allocating shots across mid-circuit assertions offers a practical way to reduce measurement costs in statistical quantum program debugging.
method: Implement four allocation strategies in the CUDA-Q-based QDB debugger.
Compare equal split, static weight allocation, adaptive entropy routing, and sequential retirement.
Use repeated circuit execution and statistical hypothesis testing to check expected qubit-state characteristics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation across different circuits under noise-free and depolarizing-noise conditions reports substantially lower total shot usage with adaptive strategies, though the abstract provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits under broader hardware noise models and larger circuits remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Shot Allocation Strategies in Debugging Quantum Circuits

title: Prototype-Guided Optimization of Quantum Data Embeddings with Linear Cost
authors: Seokhoon Jeong, Daniel K. Park
abstract: In supervised quantum machine learning with classical data, classification performance critically depends on the geometry induced by quantum data embedding. Existing data-adaptive approaches rely on pairwise fidelity evaluations between samples, which scale as $O(B^2)$ for $B$ samples and create a computational bottleneck in iterative embedding optimization. To address this issue, we propose a prototype-guided framework for efficient data-adaptive quantum embedding. Using class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness, we derive a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability and construct a prototype-based objective requiring only $O(B)$ fidelity evaluations. We integrate this objective into an end-to-end pipeline that combines task-specific quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous refinement of the data-embedding parameters. Across five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits, our method retains competitive quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) performance while reducing fidelity-evaluation cost, with particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST. Geometric analyses examine how the learned embeddings relate to kernel alignment and classification margins, revealing dataset-dependent benefits and limitations. We further derive a prototype-based classifier in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space that provides an explicit witness for the SVM objective and a low-cost proxy for model selection, and extend the framework to multiple prototypes for multimodal class structures.

infographic.key_insight: Class prototypes guide quantum data-embedding optimization using O(B) fidelity evaluations for B samples, replacing O(B²) pairwise evaluations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework reduces fidelity-evaluation cost during iterative embedding optimization while retaining competitive quantum kernel SVM performance.
method: Use class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness to derive a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability.
Combine quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous refinement of embedding parameters.
Derive an RKHS prototype classifier for low-cost model selection and extend to multiple prototypes for multimodal classes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits, the method retained competitive kernel SVM performance and showed particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits are dataset-dependent, and linear fidelity-evaluation scaling does not establish linear end-to-end runtime.
infographic.paper_title: Prototype-Guided Optimization of Quantum Data Embeddings with Linear Cost

title: Efficient Block Encodings for Ensembles of Molecular Hamiltonians
authors: Cristian L. Cortes, Andrew J. Jenkins, William Pol, Dario Rocca, Mark Steudtner, Gian-Luca R. Anselmetti
abstract: Accurately characterizing molecular properties and reactivity often requires electronic-structure calculations across an ensemble of molecular geometries. Quantum algorithms that process such ensembles coherently could address this challenge, but they require Hamiltonian block encoding circuits that combine advanced factorization techniques with sublinear scaling in ensemble size. Here, we introduce SVD-THC, which extends tensor hypercontraction to sets of Hamiltonians defined at different nuclear geometries through a singular value decomposition of the ensemble. We use SVD-THC to construct a single multiplexed block encoding circuit for all geometries in an ensemble. We then evaluate the approach on ensembles generated by varying internal rotational coordinates in 1-bromo-2-chloroethane as well as in glycine and alanine dipeptides, corresponding to established model systems for peptide conformational landscapes, with up to 5,184 geometries. Across several resolutions of the internal-coordinate grids, the Toffoli complexity of the resulting circuits grows only weakly with the number of geometries, changing by at most 12\% over grids that differ in size by up to 576$\times$. In an energy-thresholding circuit, this yields 35--200$\times$ fewer Toffoli gates than slicing together single-geometry block encodings. This approach could help make coherent processing of molecular geometry ensembles a useful primitive for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: SVD-THC enables a single multiplexed block encoding for molecular Hamiltonian ensembles, with Toffoli cost growing only weakly as more geometries are included.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method could reduce fault-tolerant quantum computing costs for coherently exploring molecular conformations and reactivity.
method: Extend tensor hypercontraction across molecular geometries using singular value decomposition.
Construct one multiplexed block encoding for the ensemble.
Use the encoding in an energy-thresholding circuit.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on 1-bromo-2-chloroethane, glycine dipeptide, and alanine dipeptide ensembles of up to 5,184 geometries showed at most 12% Toffoli-cost variation across grids differing by up to 576× in size, and 35–200× fewer Toffoli gates for energy thresholding than stitching together single-geometry encodings.
infographic.watch_item: The reported savings concern circuit resource estimates on selected molecular ensembles; generalization to broader chemical systems and practical fault-tolerant implementation remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Block Encodings for Ensembles of Molecular Hamiltonians

title: Quantum Simulation of the Static Yukawa Model via Effective Particles on a Trapped-Ion Quantum Simulator
authors: Qingfeng Wang, Christopher G. Yale, Edward C. Tortorici, Brian K. McFarland, Daniel Lobser, Melissa C. Revelle
abstract: Trapped-ion, neutral-atom, and circuit QED quantum computers naturally enable coupled qubit-boson simulations. Boson-fermion interactions arise in quantum field theory, where renormalization is required to obtain finite results. We study one of the simplest examples of a coupled fermion-boson system, the static Yukawa model, on the QSCOUT trapped-ion system. We use similarity renormalization to express the same physics in terms of effective particles described by different values of the renormalization parameter $s$. This enables us to map data taken in the window of bosonic occupancy that is experimentally accessible to larger occupancies of distinct effective particles. We use this to study strongly coupled, high-occupancy regimes despite limited readout ranges. Using a trapped-ion qubit-boson device on Sandia National Laboratories' QSCOUT platform, we demonstrate the time evolution of the static Yukawa model.

infographic.key_insight: Similarity renormalization lets a trapped-ion simulator probe strongly coupled, high-occupancy static Yukawa physics despite a limited bosonic readout range.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Effective-particle representations can extend the physics accessible on qubit–boson hardware without directly expanding its measurable occupancy range.
method: Implement coupled fermion–boson dynamics on the QSCOUT trapped-ion platform.
Use similarity renormalization to describe the same physics with effective particles at different parameter values s.
Map experimentally accessible occupancy data to larger occupancies in distinct effective-particle representations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an experimental demonstration of static Yukawa time evolution on QSCOUT, but gives no quantitative accuracy or uncertainty metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The larger-occupancy results rely on renormalization-based mapping rather than direct measurement at those occupancies.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Simulation of the Static Yukawa Model via Effective Particles on a Trapped-Ion Quantum Simulator

title: Parallel Teleportation via AME(5,2) States on IBM Quantum Hardware
authors: Zheng Liang Lim, Hoi-Kwong Lo
abstract: The five-qubit Absolutely Maximally Entangled AME$(5,2)$ state, whose every pair of qubits is maximally mixed so that all its information lives in non-local correlations, could in principle serve as a single shared quantum networking resource for teleporting two unknown qubits in parallel (each via its own Bell measurement and Pauli correction). Nonetheless, its hardware implementations remain scarce despite its theoretical importance. Here, we demonstrate parallel teleportation based on a five-qubit absolutely maximally entangled state, AME$(5,2)$, on the superconducting processor ibm_pittsburgh. We construct three-qubit Clifford decoders that extract two Bell pairs using three logical two-qubit gates for each of 60 inequivalent sender-receiver assignments. Using parallelization and classical Pauli frame post-processing, we retain reference-receiver entanglement on both channels after three teleportation rounds. With XY4 dynamical decoupling and the lowest-cost decoder, the final entanglement fidelities are $0.704\pm0.028$ and $0.680\pm0.022$, where uncertainties are pointwise $99\%$ confidence-interval half-widths over eight trials. Their lower bounds exceed the separability threshold of $1/2$. The decoder with lower circuit depth generally retains higher mean fidelity, and XY4 generally improves on XX. These results establish a hardware demonstration of two-channel entanglement transmission through repeated AME-assisted teleportation and provide compact decoding circuits for reconfigurable multipartite communication.

infographic.key_insight: A five-qubit AME state enabled parallel teleportation of two qubits on IBM quantum hardware, preserving entanglement on both channels after three rounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact Clifford decoders support reconfigurable two-channel quantum communication, with lower circuit depth and dynamical decoupling helping preserve fidelity.
method: Implemented AME(5,2)-assisted teleportation on ibm_pittsburgh.
Constructed three-qubit decoders using three logical two-qubit gates for each of 60 inequivalent sender–receiver assignments.
Combined parallel operations, classical Pauli-frame post-processing, and XY4 dynamical decoupling.
infographic.evidence_signal: With XY4 and the lowest-cost decoder, final entanglement fidelities were 0.704 ± 0.028 and 0.680 ± 0.022 across eight trials; both pointwise 99% confidence-interval lower bounds exceeded the 0.5 separability threshold.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstration is limited to two channels and three teleportation rounds; scalability to larger networks remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Parallel Teleportation via AME(5,2) States on IBM Quantum Hardware

title: Quantum algorithm for high-dimensional nonlinear stochastic differential equations based on Carleman linearization
authors: Koichi Miyamoto
abstract: Addressing nonlinear numerical problems in quantum computing remains challenging, but several approaches, including Carleman linearization (CL), have been proposed to construct quantum algorithms for such problems. In this work, we develop a CL-based method for a high-dimensional nonlinear stochastic differential equation (SDE) $\mathrm{d} \mathbf{X}_t = \left(A(t) \mathbf{X}_t + F(t) \mathbf{X}_t^{\otimes s}\right) \mathrm{d} t + B(t) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{W}_t$ for an $\mathbb{R}^N$-valued random process $\mathbf{X}_t$, aiming at quantum speed-up with respect to the dimension $N$. We introduce auxiliary processes $\mathbf{Y}^j_t$ that approximate $\mathbf{X}_t^{\otimes j}$, derive a linearized system of SDEs for them, and obtain the linear ordinary differential equation (ODE) governing their expectations. We then apply a quantum ODE solver to it and, from the resulting quantum state, extract an estimate for the expectation of a linear function of $\mathbf{X}_t$ by overlap estimation. We show that, provided the nonlinear and noise terms in the SDE are sufficiently small relative to the linear term, the CL error decreases exponentially with the truncation order $J$ in CL, and we can estimate the target expectation with a ${\rm polylog}(N)$ number of queries to unitaries encoding coefficient matrices $A$, $F$, and $B$. Finally, we also run a numerical demonstration for an SDE related to Langevin dynamics, observing the exponential decay of the CL error as $J$ increases.

infographic.key_insight: Carleman linearization enables a quantum algorithm to estimate linear observables of high-dimensional nonlinear stochastic systems with polylogarithmic query complexity in dimension N under stated conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could accelerate expectation estimation in high-dimensional stochastic models when coefficient-encoding unitaries are available and nonlinear and noise terms are sufficiently weak.
method: Introduce auxiliary processes approximating tensor powers of the stochastic state.
Truncate the Carleman hierarchy and derive a linear ODE for auxiliary expectations.
Apply a quantum ODE solver and overlap estimation to recover the target expectation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper proves exponential decay of truncation error under sufficient conditions and observes this decay numerically in a Langevin-related SDE.
infographic.watch_item: Polylogarithmic query complexity in N does not establish end-to-end speedup; coefficient encoding and other parameter dependencies must also be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum algorithm for high-dimensional nonlinear stochastic differential equations based on Carleman linearization

title: Physics-anchored residual quantum neural networks for cloud-cover parameterization
authors: Zhuo Wang, Ce Yu, Bin Yang
abstract: Compact quantum neural networks have been explored for cloud-cover parameterization, but their predictive value depends on how physical knowledge is incorporated and which classical models provide the reference. We investigate an offline residual formulation that retains a fitted \XR\ cloud-cover estimate and learns a correction to its logit in transformed target space. Using released ICON/DYAMOND-derived data, we compare ten model variants in six- and eight-input settings, with three matched replicates and 10,000 training samples per replicate. All quantum circuits use local Z readout and noiseless exact expectation values. Under a common 30-epoch protocol, residual prediction reduced physical-space test mean squared error relative to direct QNN prediction by 54.3\% and 38.8\% for six-input XYZ and ZZXY circuits, and by 49.2\% and 38.9\% for their eight-input versions. Residual QNNs also outperformed the selected compact residual multilayer perceptron in every paired replicate. A larger, longer-trained Grundner-Q1 adaptation nevertheless achieved lower error: residual Q1 reached mean MSEs of 0.00778 and 0.00791, compared with 0.01124 and 0.01082 for residual XYZ. The results support residual prediction for compact simulated QNNs within the tested budget and establish a clear boundary set by stronger classical references. They do not establish computational quantum advantage or online climate-model skill.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-anchored residual learning reduced compact QNN cloud-cover prediction error by 38.8–54.3% versus direct QNN prediction, but a stronger classical model remained more accurate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning corrections to an existing physical estimate can improve compact QNN parameterizations without replacing the baseline model.
method: Retain a fitted cloud-cover estimate and learn a correction to its logit in transformed target space.
Evaluate six- and eight-input XYZ and ZZXY quantum circuits with local Z readout and noiseless exact expectations.
Compare direct and residual QNNs against compact residual MLP and larger Grundner-Q1 classical references.
infographic.evidence_signal: On released ICON/DYAMOND-derived data with three matched replicates and 10,000 training samples each, residual XYZ achieved mean test MSEs of 0.01124 and 0.01082 versus 0.00778 and 0.00791 for residual Q1.
infographic.watch_item: Noiseless offline simulations establish neither computational quantum advantage nor skill when coupled to an online climate model.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-anchored residual quantum neural networks for cloud-cover parameterization

title: Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits over Quantum Networks
authors: Yukun Yang, Himanshu Gupta
abstract: Emerging quantum networks enable distributed quantum computing (DQC) by interconnecting modest, noisy quantum processors. However, practical deployments face tight memory budgets, probabilistic entanglement generation, and decoherence, all while serving multiple users. In realistic settings -- cloud execution, iterative/interactive workloads and concurrent jobs -- circuits do not arrive in a single batch but as a stream. This creates a fundamentally online problem: the system must react to stochastic arrivals, balance latency and throughput, and remain stable under varying loads without foresight of future jobs. We study Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits (OS-DQC) and formalize the online scheduling problem for quantum networks: circuits arrive over time and must be executed without knowledge of future arrivals. At each event time (arrival or completion), the system decides which waiting circuits to launch and how to place their qubits, while accounting for congestion from in-flight circuits and constraints due to finite memories and decoherence. The objective is to minimize the mean completion time and makespan under these physical and resource constraints.

infographic.key_insight: Distributed quantum computing needs online scheduling that responds to circuit arrivals without knowing future demand.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Quantum cloud systems must balance latency and throughput while managing limited memory, unreliable entanglement generation, and decoherence.
method: Formalize online circuit scheduling and distribution over quantum networks.
At each arrival or completion, select waiting circuits to launch and place their qubits.
Account for in-flight congestion and physical constraints while targeting mean completion time and makespan.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the problem formulation but reports no datasets, evaluation results, or quantitative performance gains.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance and stability under varying loads remain unverified by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits over Quantum Networks

title: Controlled-Z Gates via Floquet Coupling to Two Auxiliary States in Transmon Circuits
authors: Yutao Chen, Jia-Chi Zhang, Tian-Ming Li, Yu Liu, Kai Xu, Heng Fan
abstract: High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for quantum information processing. In transmon circuits, higher excited states provide additional pathways for engineering interactions within the computational subspace. Here we demonstrate controlled-Z (CZ) gates that exploit two noncomputational states, $\ket{02}$ and $\ket{20}$, through selective Floquet coupling. The nontrivial parametric modulation can activate both auxiliary transitions from $\ket{11}$ while suppressing the leading exchange between $\ket{01}$ and $\ket{10}$. Based on this approach, we develop two gate protocols: a nonadiabatic round trip through a bright auxiliary superposition and adiabatic evolution along a zero-energy dark state, both achieving average gate fidelities above $99.99\%$ in numerical simulations. Control of the modulation phase further extends the bright-state protocol to conventional and unconventional geometric CZ gates. Effective-model simulations show that unconventional control improves tolerance to residual $ZZ$ coupling and static qubit-frequency offsets relative to conventional control over the parameter ranges examined. Simulations including neighboring spectator qubits show that the original nonadiabatic bright-state and adiabatic dark-state CZ protocols retain high gate fidelities. This framework offers new routes toward the experimental realization of CZ gates and their geometric implementations.

infographic.key_insight: Selective Floquet coupling to two auxiliary transmon states enables simulated CZ gates with average fidelities above 99.99%.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Using higher transmon levels as controlled interaction pathways offers additional options for engineering high-fidelity entangling gates.
method: Parametric modulation couples |11⟩ to |02⟩ and |20⟩ while suppressing leading |01⟩–|10⟩ exchange.
Implement CZ gates through nonadiabatic bright-state round trips or adiabatic zero-energy dark-state evolution.

infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations report average fidelities above 99.99% for both core protocols; effective-model tests favor unconventional geometric control under selected errors, and spectator-qubit simulations retain high fidelities.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation remains necessary to establish performance under realistic modulation imperfections, decoherence, and leakage.

title: Bidirectional Path Integral Monte Carlo Simulation of Quantum Circuits
authors: Luis Paulo Santos, Thomas Bashford-Rogers
abstract: We propose an approximate classical algorithm for estimating quantum circuits' transition amplitudes, $\langle Ψ_f | \hat{U} | Ψ_0 \rangle$, based on Monte Carlo sums over bidirectionally sampled Feynman paths. The algorithm generates Feynman paths, i.e., sequences of intermediate computational basis states, by combining information from random walks initiated at both the input and output states, $Ψ_0$ and $Ψ_f$, respectively. It further combines this bidirectional approach with Multiple Importance Sampling, a powerful variance reduction technique that avoids variance peaks caused by divisions by the very low sampling probabilities associated with hard to reach paths. Empirical data demonstrate the superior convergence rate exhibited by the bidirectional algorithm over a unidirectional, forward-only sampling approach. This superiority is due to the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in finding and weighting paths with non-zero amplitude in an extremely sparse path space. Sum of paths algorithms exhibit very favourable space complexity. Monte Carlo replaces exhaustive enumeration of the exponentially large path space by stochastic sampling, the computational cost being determined by the variance of the estimator. This work demonstrates these two features by presenting results on very large quantum circuits, with up to 4096 qubits.

infographic.key_insight: Sampling Feynman paths from both circuit endpoints improves classical Monte Carlo estimation of quantum transition amplitudes over forward-only sampling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers memory-efficient circuit amplitude estimation, with computational cost governed by estimator variance rather than exhaustive path enumeration.
method: Launch random walks from the input and output computational basis states.
Combine forward and backward walks into bidirectionally sampled Feynman paths.
Use Multiple Importance Sampling to reduce variance from low-probability paths.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports faster empirical convergence than forward-only sampling and demonstrations on circuits with up to 4096 qubits.
infographic.watch_item: Practical runtime remains variance-dependent; the reported qubit count alone does not establish efficiency for arbitrary circuits.
infographic.paper_title: Bidirectional Path Integral Monte Carlo Simulation of Quantum Circuits

title: Measurement-efficient energy estimator for quantum chemistry of photodynamic materials
authors: Connor Lenihan, Kripa Panchagnula, Luca Erhart, Jem Guhit, Carlo A. Gaggioli, Gabriel Greene-Diniz
abstract: Accurate modelling of chemical reaction rates requires precise correlated energy differences. Quantum computing offers a potential route to their determination, but extracting energies from quantum-prepared states can demand prohibitive sampling. We demonstrate measurement-efficient correlated energy estimation using an electronically challenging H$_2$DBB--Ru model derived from a Ru-functionalized hafnium metal-organic framework relevant to radiodynamic and photodynamic therapies. The mixed estimator combines a quantum-prepared target with sparse multiconfiguration references and recovers ground-state corrections using magnitude-only compute-uncompute measurements. Analytical variance estimates predict 1.6 mHa precision with a few hundred shots, about 100 times fewer than the single-determinant formulation and three orders of magnitude fewer than optimized Hamiltonian-term sampling. With approximate targets, it reaches comparable accuracy using simpler state preparation than direct expectation-value estimation. Emulator and trapped-ion experiments on Quantinuum Helios validate the approach up to (10,10), including a 50-qubit circuit combining AI-assisted state preparation with error detection, providing a measurement-efficient route to correlated energy differences for challenging chemical problems.

infographic.key_insight: A mixed energy estimator combines quantum-prepared states with sparse multiconfiguration references to reduce sampling costs for correlated chemical energy differences.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could make quantum simulations of photodynamic materials more practical by reducing measurement demand and tolerating simpler target-state preparation.
method: Combine a quantum-prepared target with sparse multiconfiguration reference states.
Recover ground-state corrections using magnitude-only compute-uncompute measurements.
Validate with emulation and trapped-ion experiments, including AI-assisted state preparation and error detection.

infographic.watch_item: The headline shot reductions are analytical predictions; performance at larger scales will depend on reference quality, state-preparation costs, and hardware noise.
infographic.paper_title: Measurement-efficient energy estimator for quantum chemistry of photodynamic materials

title: Beyond Fidelity: Resolving Errors in Photonic Seed State Generation
authors: Sara Bartolucci, Patrick Birchall, Jacob Bulmer, Sam Gartenstein, Mihir Pant, Terry Rudolph
abstract: An important aspect of many linear optical quantum computing architectures is probabilistically generating small dual-rail qubit entangled states, or seed states. While many schemes to achieve this have been discovered, attention has been primarily focused on minimizing input resources and maximizing success probability rather than establishing a detailed understanding of linear-optical error performance. In this work, we develop a framework for resolving sensitivities to physically distinct errors in linear optical state generation, allowing us to identify precise ways in which these errors affect the properties of the output state. We use this framework to identify seed state generators in which destructive many-photon interference prevents detector loss and detector noise from causing a falsely successful heralding event. We show that this effect suppresses errors, for example cutting the effective loss on the output of particular Bell state generators in half relative to a standard scheme. We also present a new Bell state generator in which both detector loss and detector noise do not affect the quality of the output Bell state to first order, and a 4GHZ generator with >75% higher success probability than a standard circuit. In addition we provide some useful identities, bounds and invariants for studying linear optical seed state generation.

infographic.key_insight: Destructive many-photon interference can prevent certain false-success heralding events, improving photonic seed-state quality beyond what success probability alone reveals.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Error-resolved circuit design can reduce detector-induced output errors in entangled-state sources for linear optical quantum computing.
method: Develop a framework that separates sensitivities to physically distinct errors.
Identify seed-state generators where interference blocks false heralds caused by detector loss or noise.
Design and analyze improved Bell-state and four-qubit GHZ-state generators.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports halved effective output loss for particular Bell-state generators, a new Bell generator insensitive to detector loss and noise to first order, and a 4GHZ generator with over 75% higher success probability than a standard circuit.
infographic.watch_item: First-order protection does not establish immunity to higher-order or other implementation errors; the abstract does not report experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Fidelity: Resolving Errors in Photonic Seed State Generation

title: Ground-State Sampling Correspondence between Penalty-Based and Constrained Quantum Annealing
authors: Shunta Ide, Shu Tanaka
abstract: Quantum annealing generally samples degenerate ground states with nonuniform probabilities. This unfair sampling depends on how the driver Hamiltonian couples these states near the end of annealing. For combinatorial optimization problems with a cardinality constraint, the penalty method and constrained quantum annealing (CQA) differ in these couplings. The transverse-field driver of the penalty method does not directly couple feasible ground states, whereas the fully connected XY driver of CQA couples pairs of them related by a single spin exchange. We investigate how this difference affects ground-state sampling, using closed-system simulations of random graph bipartitioning instances together with degenerate perturbation theory. For the instances studied, the conditional ground-state distribution of penalty-based quantum annealing approaches that of CQA at sufficiently large penalties and long annealing times. This convergence can be explained by the effective Hamiltonian of penalty-based quantum annealing, in which virtual single-spin flips to infeasible states generate a second-order interaction proportional to the CQA driver projected onto the feasible ground-state manifold, which is the leading term of the effective Hamiltonian of CQA. In the numerical simulations, the Jensen--Shannon divergence between the conditional ground-state distributions of penalty-based quantum annealing and CQA decreases approximately as the inverse square of the penalty-to-objective energy ratio, consistent with the perturbative analysis. This correspondence between the effective Hamiltonians extends to equal-weight fixed-magnetization constraints under the same perturbative conditions, providing a common mechanism for sampling bias in the two implementations.

infographic.key_insight: At sufficiently large penalties and long annealing times, penalty-based quantum annealing approaches the same conditional ground-state sampling distribution as constrained quantum annealing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Penalty-based and constraint-preserving implementations can exhibit similar sampling bias despite using different driver Hamiltonians.
method: Simulate closed-system annealing on random graph bipartitioning instances.
Compare conditional ground-state distributions using Jensen–Shannon divergence.
Use degenerate perturbation theory to connect virtual spin flips with the projected XY driver.
infographic.evidence_signal: For the studied instances, Jensen–Shannon divergence decreases approximately as the inverse square of the penalty-to-objective energy ratio, consistent with perturbation theory.
infographic.watch_item: The correspondence requires the stated perturbative conditions and does not establish uniform sampling or robustness to hardware noise.
infographic.paper_title: Ground-State Sampling Correspondence between Penalty-Based and Constrained Quantum Annealing

title: NeST: ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles via spin shuttling
authors: Adam Siegel
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check codes now reach encoding rates up to 50% at useful distances. Their checks however are long-range group actions, not local neighbourhoods, and that connectivity has so far been supplied by neutral atoms. Silicon spin qubits offer the same primitive --- coherent transport of qubit blocks --- through electron shuttling, and on microsecond rather than millisecond timescales. They however travel along fabricated tracks rather than free space: permutations an atom array obtains by moving tweezers must here become collision-free motions on a physical lattice. We here present the first code and spin-qubit hardware co-design. We build an architecture whose geometry mimics that of a family of non-abelian groups, broad enough to host codes of excellent parameters: a hierarchy of nested conveyor-belt loops on a plain square lattice of shuttling tracks, in which every group multiplication becomes a rigid, globally controlled motion of whole qubit trains. We call it NeST, for Nested Shuttling Tracks. A code search over the family returns rate-20% mitten codes up to $[[1400,280,\leq 28]]$, and circuit-level simulations including shuttling dephasing give thresholds above $10^{-3}$ with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles, two to three orders of magnitude faster than neutral-atom implementations. Via extrapolations, we estimate that this largest code may reach a logical error probability per qubit per round of $10^{-14}$, assuming a ten-fold improvement on early shuttling demonstrations, with other physical errors at p=0.1%. Logic is compatible with NeST too: for the [[150,30,10]] code we build a code-surgery gadget in which every qubit again moves only by rigid belt motions, at no qubit cost and a 29% increase in gate layers. This demonstrates that ultra-low-overhead fault tolerance and a fast clock speed are not competing goals, and that silicon spin qubits can supply both.

infographic.key_insight: NeST co-designs high-rate quantum error-correcting codes with nested silicon-spin shuttling tracks to enable simulated stabiliser cycles below 50 μs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Rigid, globally controlled qubit-train motions could provide the long-range connectivity needed for low-overhead fault tolerance on a square lattice of fabricated tracks.
method: Map non-abelian group operations onto nested conveyor-belt loops.
Search compatible qLDPC codes and simulate circuits with shuttling dephasing.

infographic.paper_title: NeST: ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles via spin shuttling
